compared.text: `delorun changes edit-harness` makes your own copy of the installed Delo's program files and prints its folder. Each file you save, add or delete there is a change to Delo itself, listed in `delorun changes list`. With protection off, the default, the next `delorun start` applies it without review, says so, and `undo` takes it back; with protection on it waits for your review, and `show`, `apply`, `discard` and `undo` decide it as they decide a plugin's change, at a terminal. An applied change runs from Delo's next start, beside the installed release, which is never edited and is checked at every start as before; `delorun changes edit-harness --discard` takes every change to Delo itself back, even from a copy Delo can no longer read, and the next start runs the installed release unchanged. A release too large for Delo to read your copy of is refused before anything is copied. When Delo fails to start right after such a change, including when a changed file stops Delo before it starts, it starts once more without it and names it; when it does not start without it either, it names `delorun changes undo <id>` and `delorun changes edit-harness --discard`. Safe mode runs the installed release without any of your changes to it. `delorun verify` and `delorun doctor` list the files you changed and never report a pass when the files Delo would run with your changes differ from what you applied.

Installing Delo with `npx delorun` downloads the release it publishes, checks every file against the signed manifest and the public release log, and refuses to install anything that does not match. The runtime it installs is kept and reused, so starting Delo again needs no network.

`--release` is refused, with both versions named, when a runtime is already installed, instead of being ignored. `--` ends the launcher's own options, so the runtime keeps its own `--release` and `--profile`.
An install whose download fills the disk stops with the launcher's own message instead of a raw file-system error.

Installing Delo with `npx delorun` now prints one line for each step it takes: which release it found, that the signature checked out, whether the public release log agreed, the size of the download, and the install itself. If the release log or its witness cannot be reached, has not cosigned the log's latest checkpoint, or only cosigned it long ago, the install says why, warns that the release has not been checked against the log, goes on with the release's signature, and checks again at the next connection. A log or witness that answers and disagrees with the release, or whose cosignature does not verify, still stops the install.

Running `npx delorun` on a Node older than the one Delo needs now stops at once with one line that names the version Delo needs and where to get it, instead of failing with an error from inside the program.

When the installed Delo fails its start check because its files changed, the launcher says so in one line and, if the version before your last update is still installed and intact, starts that version's `delorun recover rollback` to take you back; otherwise it stops with the reason as before.

Unpacking the runtime writes several files at once while it reads the archive, so installing or updating Delo spends about half as long unpacking: about 9 seconds instead of 18 for a full-size runtime on a busy computer.

Delorun 0.1.0 runs on Linux (x64 and arm64) and on Windows through WSL2. A release publishes runtimes for Linux x64 and Linux arm64 only. Running `npx delorun` or `delorun update` on native Windows stops before downloading anything and says Delorun 0.1.0 runs in WSL2, with a link to the guide's WSL2 steps. On a Mac it stops the same way and says macOS joins in a later release. A computer whose platform a release does not list still stops with `PLATFORM_NOT_RELEASED`.

`delorun verify` checks the installed release: its files against the signed manifest, the manifest's signature and timestamp, and the release's entry in the public transparency log, in a tree the log and a witness both signed. It trusts only the release root the launcher shipped and the roots an install walked from it, prints one line per check with a summary that says it is not a full verification of Delo, and exits 1 when a check fails or the release signature could not be confirmed for a reason other than an unreachable log. It also names the directory of the launcher's roots it trusted and the release channel and log the installing launcher recorded. `--json` prints the same report for a machine, and `--offline` skips the log.

The installer, the launcher's start and `delorun verify` run one release-log check and keep one record of the newest log checkpoint they verified. A log that cannot be reached, answers with an error or is not signed by the log's key leaves the release unchecked and never stops a start; a log that is signed and then contradicts an earlier checkpoint, serves a broken proof or carries an invalid witness signature stops the start and names `delorun verify`. The check gives up after 90 seconds, and a running Delo retries an unchecked release every 15 minutes.

A checkpoint stored by an earlier install is kept as the rollback floor only when the log proves it a prefix of its latest checkpoint; otherwise it is replaced, and the check says so instead of resetting the floor silently. `delorun verify` says since when a release has stayed unchecked.

`npx delorun@latest repair` replaces a program that will not start with a verified release and keeps your chats, settings, keys, devices and trust records. It asks you first in a terminal, refuses while Delorun runs, refuses to put an older release over chats a newer release wrote, and keeps the old program in `runtimes.set-aside-<time>/`, which `delorun recover status` lists. `--restore-copy`, `--from` and `--reset-trust` cover the harder cases. Each start now records which release wrote your data in `data-format.json`.

`delorun update` lists each change you made to Delo itself and says whether it carries over to the new release. A change carries as it is when the new release left that file alone. When the new release changed the file without touching your lines, the two merge into a file neither had: `delorun update` prints its diff against the new release's file, and only you confirm it, not `--yes`. When the two overlap, the new release's file runs and yours is kept beside it as `<file>.mine` in your copy of the new release, and `--yes` does not confirm such an update either. An update refuses while changes to Delo itself wait for your review, or when your copy of Delo cannot be read, naming `delorun changes edit-harness --discard` and `delorun changes list`; it refuses before switching when what it would do with your changes no longer matches the report you confirmed, and asks you to run `delorun update` again. Going back to the previous release runs your changes to it again.

`delorun update --from <folder or https address>` installs a release from files you downloaded from its release page when the release channel cannot be reached. It checks signatures, the release log and digests like a channel update. If the channel cannot confirm the release is current, it asks first in a terminal; `--yes` and a missing terminal refuse. A release below the one you run is refused. `npx delorun@latest repair --release <older> --from <folder>` asks in the same way. A repair now marks the whole home while it runs, so no Delorun starts meanwhile, not even for a new profile, and cannot run the program being set aside. A start during a repair says "Delorun is being repaired; wait for it to finish".

Delo tells you when a newer release exists: once a day, and at start when a day has passed, it checks your release channel's signed files and, when a newer release is out, prints one line in the terminal and shows a quiet notice in the studio's sidebar with the new version, whether it is a security fix, how many of your plugins it would turn off, and the command to run. Nothing is downloaded or installed until you run `delorun update`, and you can dismiss the notice for that version.

The check sends nothing about you or your plugins; the release hosts see your computer's address. Setup asks whether to check for new releases under More settings, and `delorun setup privacy`, `--no-update-check` and an answers document's `updateCheck` turn it off; turned off in setup, it makes no request at all, not even at the first start. Turn it off later in Settings → General → Updates, and run it yourself any time with `delorun update --check`. `delorun update --report` shows everything an update would change, plugin by plugin, without applying it.

`delorun update` fetches the newest release on your channel, checks it, shows what it would change in your profile before anything changes, and applies it once you confirm. Running chats finish first, and an update whose new version fails its health check goes back on its own and names the check it failed; a plugin the report disables does not count as a failure when its rows are gone, and neither does a Docker socket that appeared, or a Docker context you switched, since Delo started; a new version whose sandbox would protect less than the one it replaces goes back too. Updates come from the channel the launcher that installed Delo was built for; no environment variable or setting moves it. Delo keeps your profile's history with git, so an update and a rollback say so and stop before they fetch or change anything when git is not installed. A release that does not verify, a release channel that cannot be reached, or an update the home process could not finish, ends with a sentence that says what happened and what you can do.

While an update or `delorun stop` waits for running chats to finish, a new message starts no turn: the chat shows that Delo is updating and that the message was not sent, so you send it again once Delo is back, and the wait ends once the running chats end. Background jobs count as running chats, and stopping with `--now` cancels them too.

Before an update applies, Delo works out what the new release would change in the person's profile: each plugin it would disable or remove and why, judged exactly as Delo judges a plugin when it installs or starts one, so a plugin that names its DeepSeek Harness versions only through its peer dependencies is not shown as kept when the next start would turn it off, each bundle that leaves the bundle list or cannot load, and each row and Include that loads a plugin the update disables. The report marks every prediction it could not fully make from metadata it could read, so those are never counted as safe, and it shows both the CLI home's and the desktop Host's versions and update states, because the two update independently. Nothing applies until the person confirms, and `delorun update --yes` will not confirm a report that disables or removes anything or rests on metadata Delo could not read.

When an update changes the format of your chat data, the report says so and Delo copies your chats and workspaces first, unless you choose to continue without the copy. Going back restores that copy and keeps the chats written since in a set-aside folder; nothing is deleted.

`delorun recover status` says whether your last update committed, was rolled back or has not committed, lists the update you can go back from and every kept copy and set-aside folder with its size, `delorun recover rollback` goes back, `--profile-only` restores only your profile, and `delorun recover discard` removes a kept folder you no longer need. Delo's home log records each step of a rollback as it records an update's, so `delorun logs home` shows where a slow rollback spent its time.

An update or a rollback checks every release against the release roots of the launcher that started Delo, so a root file replaced under the home is not trusted; a Delo started without its launcher refuses to update or roll back and says to start it with the launcher. A studio that takes long to shut down for an update is waited for instead of ending Delo in the middle of the switch, and one that does not shut down ends the update with nothing changed and Delo running again.

Contributors can measure where a person waits on Delo with `pnpm run benchmark:delo`: install and setup, start and stop, the everyday commands, `delorun update`, `update --check` and rollbacks step by step, recovery, export, import and the trash, plugins, a chat turn without a model, and the studio in a headless browser, all on local releases in throwaway homes with no network, with a mode that fails when a step exceeds its recorded ceiling.

`delorun update --report` and `delorun update` show, under a plugin the update turns off because its DeepSeek Harness version range excludes the new release, the command that accepts the risk for that exact version and say that the health check after the switch rolls the update back if the plugin then fails to load. A new guide page, "Update Delorun with many plugins", walks through saving, checking, updating and going back.

`delorun recover discard runtimes.set-aside-<time>` removes the program store that `delorun repair` set aside. It stopped with a permission error because the installed program's folders are read-only.

`delorun repair` refuses to start an older program over chats when the home records which release wrote them and the release's data formats cannot be compared (`DATA_UNREADABLE`), and `--restore-copy` refuses a copy whose formats are newer than the release reads (`DATA_COPY_NEWER`). A restored copy's facts become the home's data-format record. A release signed by a local release build is refused from a `--from` folder as well when the launcher trusts the production keys, and `repair` reads the floor from the channel the home installed from.
When a repair was killed during its download, the next start or repair names the set-aside program store (`runtimes.set-aside-*`) and prints the command that puts the old programs back.
`delorun update --from` with a folder that does not exist now says the folder does not exist and that nothing was installed, instead of reporting a failed download.
An update that fails its health check rolls back on its own even when the new release was stopped while it wrote a profile lock file.

Starting an installed runtime does not trust a release root merely because a file under `~/.delo/trust/` names a newer version: the launcher keeps the root chain the install walked, checks that it leads from a root the launcher carries, and otherwise stops and offers a reinstall. It starts a runtime only when the release root the home stored is one the launcher ships.
An installed runtime is made read-only before its files are hashed, so nothing can change a file between its check and the mode that protects it.

The runtime starts without the `NODE_OPTIONS`, `NODE_PATH`, `LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` and `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` variables that the shell passed in, so the shell that started `delorun` cannot stand between the runtime and the connections it verifies. A profile name that would leave the Delo home is refused before anything is read.

The release-log check accepts every consistency proof the log serves and refuses only one that does not reproduce both tree roots. It also refuses a bundle that names a different manifest file than the release's own, a release version that is not a version, and a checkpoint that no listed witness has signed, even when the trusted root carries no witness requirement of its own. A log entry whose signing key cannot be read says why in its refusal.

The Linux runtime's sandbox launcher and file-lock addon are compiled from the release's own tagged source in a pinned toolchain without network access, so a rebuild of the release reproduces them byte for byte, signing covers them and the release's software bill of materials names the compiler packages that built them.

A Delo release and its freshness timestamps are signed only with keys the public repository records as Delo's production keys, so nothing is signed until those keys are recorded. A release is signed only when its version tag carries the signature of a release signer that the release branch of the public repository lists, not a local copy of that list, and the tagged code is on the release branch, and only when the `delorun` npm package it records, by name, version and checksum, is the package the release built. Until install scripts are rebuilt and compared like the rest of a release, no release lists one.
A test release built on someone's own computer can never be signed with Delo's real release keys, so a launcher that trusts Delo's releases never accepts one.

Each start checks the installed release under the newest release root the launcher ships, never an older root the home stored, so a signing key a newer root revoked stops the start. The launcher passes on no `DELO_LAUNCHER_` setting it inherited.

A start stops when the release-log bundle kept beside an installed release is missing, instead of starting with a warning; the message names the missing file and offers `delorun recover rollback` or putting the file back, and `delorun verify` fails on it as before.
A launcher that installs from Delo's published release channel refuses a release that the local release tool built.

`delorun update` never moves to a release lower than the one running: a channel or a request that names a lower release is refused before anything is downloaded, and `delorun recover rollback` stays the only way back.
The update report says when the release log could not be reached as the release was installed, instead of showing its log check as passed, and `delorun update --yes` does not confirm such a release.

The `delorun` command keeps your data in your own Delo home, `~/.delo` or the directory `DELO_HOME` names, readable only by you, and never touches DeepSeek Harness's `~/.dsh`. Its first run sets up the command-line profile; after that it starts Delo in your terminal and opens the studio. Only one Delo runs per profile.

If the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` sets the sandbox row's `runnerCommand` or `runnerFailureSignatures`, `delorun start` refuses with an error naming them and asking for their removal: your home's protection runs through the sandbox's built-in runner selection.

`delorun import-home` copies your DeepSeek Harness home, `~/.dsh` or the folder `--from` names, into your Delo home. It only reads `~/.dsh`, which stays exactly as it was. After one yes it copies your chats, exactly as they were saved, the images and files they refer to, and your workspace list.

Then it asks about each of these on its own, and each starts on no: your profiles, your settings, your `AGENTS.md` instructions, your skills and your DeepSeek key. It shows each before it asks: each profile's plugins as carried, to install, added or not carried, the exact settings that would land, the first lines of your instructions, each skill's description, and your stored keys by name and never by value. `--dry-run` shows the preview and writes nothing.

Only settings that change how Delo looks and your default model by name carry over: your theme and fonts, how chats and the composer show things, and your language. Every other setting is held back even after a yes, because it could run code, send your requests or key elsewhere, or switch off a protection; the preview lists each with the reason, and the import writes them where nothing reads them. A profile lands with its plugin list alone: no install script, lockfile, build approval or plugin from a path. A profile named `headless` stays behind, because `delorun headless` sets up its own, and so does a profile whose name Delo can't start, such as one with a capital letter or a dot.

Setup asks "Copy your DeepSeek Harness chats, attachments and workspace list?" after its preview when `~/.dsh` exists and your Delo home has no chats yet, starting on no, and copies only those. `delorun import-home` copies the rest.

The preview lists every workspace with its folder. A workspace in your home folder itself, a hidden folder of it such as `.ssh`, the root of your disk or a Harness home stays behind with its chats, and so does a chat that works outside its workspace's folder or stopped in the middle of a turn. Before each question the import shows the whole text that would land, a page at a time.
A chat that ran with full access in DeepSeek Harness opens on the safer preset until you allow full access for its workspace in Delo.

The import refuses a Delo home that already holds chats unless you add `--merge`, and never overwrites a chat, attachment or workspace. Links, pipes, other drives, files linked to something outside `~/.dsh`, attachments whose content does not match their name, and names DeepSeek Harness does not write are never followed or copied; no plugin, script or install runs; it copies at most 4 GiB unless `--max-size` gives more; and if your computer stops during an import, the next start of Delo removes the part it had copied.

After the import, `delorun plugin --profile <name> install` installs each profile's plugins; the import prints the command for every profile that needs it, and a plugin's install script runs only after you approve it.

`delorun setup` asks which model provider Delorun uses: Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google Gemini, Groq, Mistral, Moonshot AI, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together AI, xAI or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, listed by name, or none for now, which changes no provider setting and says which model new chats still start on. DeepSeek works without any extra install, and so does every other provider in the list.

For each provider setup asks where its key comes from, typed now or read from the provider's variable at each start, and the model new chats start on, beginning on a current general model of that provider; an OpenAI-compatible endpoint also takes its base URL, without a user name, password, query or fragment and with a warning for plain http to another computer, and its model id. Setup keeps DeepSeek's default model and asks the model of every other provider; `delorun setup key` asks it for DeepSeek too.

A typed key is checked with one request for the provider's model list, or OpenRouter's key details, to the provider's own address, never a completion; a failed check says why and lets you enter the key again or continue with the key marked not verified.

`delorun setup --yes` sets up no provider unless `--provider <id>` names one, with `--model`, `--base-url` for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and `--key-env` for another variable, and says how to add one when none is named. `delorun setup key` takes the same flags on a profile that is set up and asks nothing. A key is never taken from the command line.

Setup writes what the studio's Settings → Models and the model picker save, so the studio shows the provider and model setup chose; DeepSeek with its own variable and default model leaves the profile as DeepSeek Harness composes it.

You can run setup again if you change your mind. `delorun setup` on a finished setup, in a terminal, asks every question again with your current choices selected, keeps your saved key, marks the answers you change and writes only those. In the studio, Settings → General → Run setup again opens the first-run steps on your current choices.

`delorun setup` asks the model provider with its key and how careful prompts should be, and its More settings choice asks whether Delorun keeps running in the background and the profile's name and port. Changes protection is asked there too: it holds changes to your plugins and to Delorun itself for your review, and setup never turns it off. A typed key is checked with one live request to the provider before it is stored, and a failed check says why and lets you enter the key again or continue. Every question can return to the one before it, and a review screen lists the answers before anything is written.
"Ask me first" and "Ask less (like DeepSeek Harness)" take effect: they set Delo's consent and permission defaults to their Delo or stock values in the new profile.
`delorun setup <section>` runs one section again, and `delorun setup --list` lists them.

A terminal setup ends by printing the next steps and starts nothing; `delorun` starts Delorun in the background, which keeps running after the terminal closes, with the commands `delorun status`, `delorun logs --follow` and `delorun stop`.

`delorun setup --yes` applies every default; `delorun setup --config <file>` applies an answers document. Neither form turns on reach or credential forwarding, and `--check-key` checks the key with one live request.
`delorun setup` does not ask about the two upstream opt-ins, desktop analytics and DeepSeek's session-log upload. Both stay off, and Settings → Privacy changes them.
An interrupted setup resumes at the step it did not finish, and a finished setup is left unchanged.
Setup from a source checkout adds Delo's bundle to the new profile, so the Privacy section in Settings loads on the first start without a manual step.

The studio's first minute is one short guide that ends in a chat. Welcome sets the language, shows the preview notice and tests each model key with the provider's free model list, so nothing is spent; you can add or change a provider without leaving the guide. Look shows a small chat in the colours you pick. Agents offers Claude Code and Codex, says whether each is signed in on this computer, and asks you to confirm what adding one means: when an agent starts from a chat Delo asks on this computer first unless you allowed it for that workspace, a phone cannot answer, read-only chats never start one, runs stay in the chat's workspace and stop after 30 minutes, and Settings → External agents revokes it; it runs outside Delo's sandbox with its own sign-in and billing. Recommended plugins puts the plugins that fit your setup first. Phone access, while it is off, checks Tailscale step by step and gives the commands to copy. Workspace opens your first chat in the default workspace, a folder you choose, or a repository cloned from Git; a clone never asks for a password, refuses an address with a sign-in in it, runs none of your Git hooks or filters, shows its progress and says why it failed. Ready lists what you set and opens the chat with starting prompts that fit the folder and fill in the message box for you to send. The studio's own notice about a missing default workspace waits while the guide is open. Settings → General → Getting started shows the guide again. With no working model key, a calm line above the message box says "Add a model key to start chatting" and opens Settings → Models; the studio no longer opens upstream's "Add an API key" dialog.

`delorun setup` opens with "How will you use Delorun?": just me on this computer, also from my phone or another device, or scripts and automation. The answer sets the defaults and decides which questions come next, so most people answer three: the model provider and its key, and how much Delorun asks. The review screen lists every answer, including the release check and the prompts answer, and its More settings choice asks the rest. This replaces the Quick or Full choice.

Every choice shows what it does, who it suits and how to change it later, and the recommended one is marked. The prompts choices are Ask me first, Ask less (like DeepSeek Harness) and Never ask (dangerous), which stays the third option with its two confirmations.

Each provider's key question names the provider's key page where one is known, says what an environment variable is, and warns at once, with the fix, when the variable you pick is not set in your terminal.

Setup ends by printing the next steps and starts nothing: `delorun` to start and open the studio, the install guide's section on your first chat, and `delorun setup <section>` to change an answer. Ctrl-C exits with code 130 and says nothing was saved. Choosing Back at the dangerous-mode confirmation returns to the prompts question.

An answers document may carry `"useCase": "local" | "remote" | "automation"`; without it, `local` is used. An answers record written by an earlier setup, with or without a Quick or Full `mode`, still reads.
Setup ends by saying once that Delo is running in the background, and the review screen says when the key check failed and the key is not verified.
In a source checkout, the package manager's output while Delo links its parts into the profile goes to the home process's log, and the terminal shows one progress line.
`delorun status` prints the studio's address, without any token, and "Run delorun open to open the studio in your browser."

`delorun setup` installs the `delorun` command at the exact version of the launcher you ran, `npm install -g delorun@<version>`, never whatever version npm serves as newest, and offers no install when that version is unknown. `delorun verify` prints the launcher's version with the integrity the signed release lists for it, which you compare with `npm view delorun@<version> dist.integrity` as the Trust page describes.

Picking Full access in a chat whose folder does not have full access shows what it means before anything changes: one sentence on what agents can then do, one on the risk, and under Details the folder and what full access reaches: your files, Delo's home with its keys and tokens, the Docker supervisor and Delo's update channel. It is the only dialog the permission control shows for Full access, and it asks you to tick that you understand the risks before Allow full access is enabled. Allow full access records your answer and switches the chat; Cancel leaves it in the sandbox. In a folder that already has full access, or a chat without a folder, the same dialog asks "Switch this chat to full access?" with the same tick and records nothing.

When an agent asks to run something outside the sandbox, its approval card has three buttons: Reject, Allow once, and Allow for this chat. Allow for this chat switches the chat to the permission the request asked for, so later commands in the chat run without asking, and allows the request. For full access it shows the same single dialog first, and Cancel leaves the request waiting. You lower the permission again in the composer. A chat already at or above the requested permission shows only Allow once. Once you rejected the request, or it ended, the button is greyed out and switches nothing, also when you confirm the dialog it opened. If the switch is refused, the request stays waiting and the reason shows under the buttons.

Settings, Permissions lists everything you allowed, each with a one-click Revoke. Full access lists the folders that have it, where new chats start with full access; revoking puts the folder's open full-access chats back on the safer permission within a second, in every running profile, and the other folders sit behind a disclosure where you can allow it. MCP servers lists the local servers waiting for your OK, with what changed (a new server, or its command, arguments, folder or which environment variables changed since you allowed it, or the file or folder it points to changed), the servers you declined or revoked, which stay stopped and quiet until you allow them, and the servers you allowed, each remembered on its own; revoking one stops it until you allow it again. Each answer's result shows under the section's introduction.

Review on a waiting MCP server says what allowing it does, the exact file it runs and the folder it runs in, and its risk, what changed, and under Details its command, arguments, folder, the file, command shell and folder they point to, and environment variables, showing a value only for variables that change what runs, such as `PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS` or `LD_PRELOAD`. Allow and start starts it without restarting Delo, and if the file or folder changed since you looked, nothing is allowed and the review shows the new one; Decline keeps it stopped.
When an MCP server waits for your OK, a notice names it, and "Review and allow this server" opens its review, then the next waiting server's.

These answers are given only on the home's own computer. On a phone or another device, the approval card, the notice, Settings, Permissions and the full-access explanation say to approve at your computer and offer no button; the phone sees only the names of the waiting servers. With "Ask less (like DeepSeek Harness)" prompts, Settings, Permissions says the profile does not ask, and the permission picker switches as DeepSeek Harness does.

The sidebar's Plugins page offers a cost meter, under Components on the Delo studio page: turn it on and each chat shows an estimate of what it has cost under the composer, and the breakdown names each model's requests, tokens and cost, with the chats a chat started added up under it.

You can bring the chats you had on chat.deepseek.com into Delorun. Export them from the website, turn on DeepSeek chat import under Plugins, More, then upload the file with the button beside New session; the first-run guide's Recommended plugins step offers the same switch. The plugin is off until you turn it on, and only you at the computer can import.

The first-run guide's Recommended plugins step now also offers the Thinking tab and the cost meter. Both are off until you press Turn on, and each starts at once, with no restart. They stay under Plugins → Delo studio → Components too.

When the studio cannot start because a plugin fails to load or the page does not open within 30 seconds, and always at `/recovery`, a recovery screen shows what failed and your recent changes, and lets you turn off a plugin, undo a change or start in safe mode, in English or Chinese. These actions work only in a browser on the computer Delo runs on; a remote session can read the screen and is told "This needs you at your computer."
Settings lists Changes under Data, after Trash, so the review of plugin and harness changes is one click from the navigation.

Settings has a Setup versions page that lists the versions Delorun keeps of your setup, newest first, with the current one marked and what made each: an update, a save by you or a switch. Save this setup, with an optional name, keeps a version; What changes shows, in plain words, which plugins, bundles, settings and version exemptions switching to a version would change; Switch to this version saves your current setup as a version first, so switching back is switching to that version, and then tells you to restart Delorun to run it. The page uses the same history as `delorun recover`. Saving and switching work only in the studio on your computer: a phone or other device sees the list and the changes and is told to do it at your computer.

In the studio's collapsed sidebar, moving the pointer to the rail — or to the left edge where the desktop hides the rail — opens the full sidebar over the page after a short pause, without moving what you are reading and without pinning it open. It closes again a moment after the pointer leaves (moving back in keeps it open), on Escape, or when keyboard focus leaves it, and hovering one of the rail's own controls never opens it, so every rail click still does what it did.

A Changes section in Settings lists the changes to your plugins that wait for your review, the changes a failed start left out, your agent's plugin requests and your recent changes. Review shows a change's folder, its files, a summary of what it can do with the reminder that the summary helps you read the change and is not a protection, the files the diff does not show, and the diff; Apply asks a second time and names what the summary found when it flagged anything. Discard, Undo and Apply again work from the same section, Start working loads a plugin's edits live, and Done shows the folder's version with its diff and approves exactly that version. An agent's plugin request can be applied there after a second confirmation that says Delo cannot show what it installs before it runs. The section shows the protection setting with the terminal command that changes it, and with protection off says that changes load without your review, and your changes to Delo itself with their diff and the terminal command that decides each. While a work session lasts, a badge at the foot of the sidebar names the plugin. A browser that is not on the computer Delo runs on sees everything with every action disabled and "This needs you at your computer."

The studio opens in Delo's look: a softer palette with a choice of accents and themes, Delo's typefaces, a density and a contrast setting, under Settings → Appearance, and a Conversation page for how chats are displayed. One switch in Settings → General → Look turns every Delorun addition to the studio off and shows the stock DeepSeek Harness look; with the stock look, one row under Settings → General turns the Delorun look back on.
A profile set up with an earlier Delo turns to the Delo look at its next start; one switch in Settings → General → Look turns it back to the stock look.
Under the Delo look, a new chat's empty screen shows the Delo wordmark above its headline.
Under the Delo look, the page shown while the studio loads names Delo instead of HARNESS.

The sidebar lists chats as cards with their status, sorted with pinned chats first, with search, a workspace filter, Alt and a digit to jump to one of the first nine chats, and an undo for each change you make from the list. Each workspace can have its own icon (letters, a glyph, an emoji or a generated pattern, in its own colour and shape), and the top of the sidebar can show header art, drawn in full behind the white name and sidebar button, which a thin dark edge keeps readable on any scene; both are chosen under Settings → Sidebar. Plugins, Automation tasks and More sit as icon buttons in the sidebar's bottom row, beside Settings.

The sidebar's Plugins page offers a Thinking tab, under Components on the Delo studio page: turn it on and the right sidebar can show the model's reasoning and reply one word at a time as it writes them, at a pace you choose, with a delay behind the model if you like.

The studio's sidebar foot shows how much of this Delo was checked: a small badge reads verified only when every runtime file was hashed by a full check and the release log, the plugins and your changes all check out, reads "Checked at start" after an ordinary start, which hashes only part of the runtime, turns red for a failed check and amber for an unknown release, an unchecked release log, a plugin changed after its install or a critical advisory, and shows your own changes, including those waiting for your review, as a plain count. It opens a panel with the four rows, their details, and Check now, which runs `delorun verify` through the launcher, so every runtime file is hashed before the check runs, and shows how long it has run. A phone or laptop you approved for remote access sees the panel read-only; Check now runs only on the computer Delorun runs on. The panel says that these checks run with your access, so a program running as you can change them.

Settings opens as one larger panel with its pages grouped by topic and a search field that finds pages and settings by name, in English and Chinese. A section from a plugin that the grouping does not name appears under More.

Settings is arranged in five groups. General holds a General page (language, look, updates with the release check and the current versions, keyboard shortcuts, getting started and the coding view), Appearance (colours, then text and density), Sidebar, a Conversation page for how chats are displayed, and Chat (composer, links and usage). Agent holds Models, Modes, Tools and Plugins; Safety holds Permissions (new chats, full access and MCP servers), External agents (the switch that asks before an external agent runs, its run time limit and the agents you allowed), Network and Privacy; then come Devices, and Data with Trash and About, which now lists the licences and project links.
Every Settings page uses sentence-case headings, two- and three-way choices are segmented controls that work as radio buttons, and Thinking under Conversation is a menu.
A third-party plugin can give its Settings sections a group of its own, titled with the plugin's name; sections nothing places appear under Other.
The studio's sidebar shows Delo's hex jack mark, its centre in your accent colour, and the product name, Delo, as its brand. The DeepSeek Harness mark and name no longer appear in Delo's studio.

The studio's preview notice is Delo's own. It says that Delo is a pre-release community fork of DeepSeek Harness, built independently of DeepSeek. The browser tab title and the home-screen name read Delo.
A sign-in link you tap in a message or on a web page now signs you in, and a browser that loads the link ahead of time no longer uses it up. A link already used or past its minute still fails.

Onboarding on a phone shows a welcome line, a one-line note in place of the computer's phone access steps, a shorter key field hint that says where the key comes from, and larger tap targets. Onboarding and the greeting say Delorun.
The studio no longer asks for the update notice when the release check is off, so the browser console stays clean.

The Plugins page's install guide names `delorun plugin add` and `delorun plugin remove`, the commands Delo has, and asks for the full path of a plugin's folder, which is the only kind of folder path the studio can install from.
The browser tab is titled "Delo", not "DSH Local Build", and the studio's stored look is applied before the first paint, with no flash of the stock sidebar.
After you trash the chat that is open, the main pane shows a new chat and the keyboard returns to the message box.

The guide's option chips are one labelled group you move through with the arrow keys, and its two "Add" buttons have distinct names. The page has a `main` landmark, "Search chats" and the message box show a focus ring, "Reconnecting..." is announced politely, and Escape closes the phone-width sidebar drawer.

The studio you open on the computer that runs it no longer reads "Disconnected" when that computer has no network, such as with Wi-Fi off. It stays connected, because it never needed the network, and it no longer makes a request that only a phone or other device could use, which showed as a failed request in the browser's console.

Delo's setup no longer offers DeepSeek account sign-in, the account entry in the menu is gone, and so are the account's Usage and Top-up pages. Use your own DeepSeek API key, which Delo's model settings still accept. The account pages stay in upstream's code and are not reachable from Delo's default setup.

`delorun export <chat-or-workspace> --out <file>` writes a chat, or a workspace with its chats and their attachments, as an archive signed by your home. It warns about secrets it finds in the chat history, naming each by kind and never by value, and writes nothing until you confirm.

`delorun import <file>` checks the whole archive before it writes anything, shows who signed it and what it holds, and imports it after you confirm. An archive whose signature does not verify, whose bytes disagree with its manifest, whose paths leave the destination, that holds a link, or that is past its size or compression limits is refused; an archive from a home you do not know is imported only after you type its key's fingerprint, and an unsigned one only after you accept it unverified. Imported chats are kept apart and stay out of every model request.

Importing an archive brings a person's exported chats, attachments and workspaces into the home in one step that writes nothing until the whole archive has been checked: a path that climbs out of the destination, an absolute path, a link, a device, an archive past its size or compression limits and an archive whose bytes disagree with its manifest are all refused before anything is staged. The import states whether the archive's signature is verified, and shows the customisation the archive carries as a diff before any row is applied; an export warns about the secrets it finds in chat history before it writes the file.

An archive that hides a configuration expression behind JSON escapes is refused, so a customisation value that reads as a tagged expression is caught after it is decoded as well as in the file's raw text.
An archive with two entries whose names are the same word written in different Unicode forms is refused, because both would land on one file.

A new Delorun home has a default workspace on every platform: `Delo/default-workspace` in your documents folder when the computer reports one that is not your home folder, otherwise `Delo` directly in your home folder. `delorun start` picks the folder, and it is created when the studio first needs it. Restating the `workspace-controller` row in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` with your own `defaultWorkspaceDirectory` chooses another folder.

A chat can be snoozed until later or settled when it is done, from its menu or its card; it moves to a folded Snoozed or Settled shelf at the bottom of the chat list and comes back when its snooze ends or when you send it a message. The snooze times and an optional rule that settles chats left idle for some days are set under Settings → Sidebar. The states are kept on your computer and never reach the model.

Deleting a chat or a workspace now moves it to the trash: "Move to trash" in a chat's or a workspace's menu archives its chats, stops their running work and takes them out of the sidebar. The new Trash section in Settings lists what was deleted with the days each item has left, restores an item where it was, and deletes one or every item forever from every place Delo keeps it, with an offer to clear the operational logs at once. Items older than 30 days are deleted when Delo starts. `delorun trash list`, `restore`, `purge` and `empty` do the same from the terminal while Delo is stopped.

Trash deletes a chat or a workspace into a 30-day retention, restores it before the retention ends, and purges it from every store that holds its content: the full-text index, the session generations, the attachments, the spill files and the browser drafts. It offers to clear the affected process logs, current and rotated, at once.
Permanently deleting a chat also removes the copy the session list keeps for it, so the chat's title, first message, plan, goal and todos no longer stay on disk after the purge.

A folder you open now starts on the safer permission, so a chat can write inside it and asks before doing more; turning on full access for a folder takes one answer covering that folder, and a chat whose folder was never answered stays in the sandbox even when something tries to switch it.

Choosing the safer permission for a folder again withdraws that folder's full-access answer, so turning full access back on asks once more, and puts the folder's other open full-access chats back on the safer permission within a second, in every running profile. A chat picking full access after another profile or `delorun workspace full-access` withdrew it asks again.

A code run whose execution process ends on its own now reports that process's own exit status every time. A busy machine no longer replaces it with the termination signal we sent to a process that was already stopping.

A damaged workspace list no longer leaves the studio empty. Delorun starts with every workspace record it can read, sets the rest aside in a dated file next to the list (it never deletes one), and logs where it is. It also keeps the previous good copy of the list, `delorun doctor` checks the list, and `delorun recover workspaces` brings the previous copy back after asking you. See [The workspace list](../../docs/guide/troubleshooting.md#the-workspace-list).
The agent can rename a workspace with the new `rename_workspace` tool, after you allow it, instead of editing files by hand.

When some workspace records were set aside, the studio says so above the message box, names the file and points to `delorun doctor`; you can dismiss it. A `rename_workspace` call in a chat shows the old and new name, or why it was refused.

With changes protection on, before the agent first writes to the folder of a plugin you approved, the chat asks you, names the plugin and shows the diff, because the agent is changing what your harness runs; once you allow it, the rest of that chat's writes to the plugin go ahead, and what it wrote still waits for your review in `delorun changes`. A link or a `..` in the path asks the same way.

With changes protection on, when the agent asks to install, update or remove a plugin, nothing is installed or removed: the request waits in `delorun changes` and the studio's Changes section for you to apply or discard it at your computer, and the agent is told so. With protection off, the default, the agent's plugin requests run as in DeepSeek Harness and a plugin it installs from a folder is recorded as loaded without review. Applying a plugin from a folder adds it with nothing loaded, and its content waits for your review as its own change.

With setup's Dangerous answer on, a phone or browser signed in over remote access, with its unlock running, can do what the computer does: change the settings and plugin rows the computer alone changes with the other answers, run any slash command, loosen the permission new chats start in, answer the questions for MCP servers, external agents and a workspace's network, give the approvals that reserve full access, use terminals, save or remove provider keys (a saved key is never sent back), open a chat's folder in an application on the computer, and read files outside the chat's workspace. A workspace's full access that a device turns on ends with the mode, while what you set at the computer stays. Only the computer turns the mode on, approves a new device or an unlock, removes a device, changes the remote-access settings or signs a device in. Settings, Permissions now shows `delorun setup prompts` as code in the Dangerous mode card.

With setup's Dangerous answer on, any chat can switch to full access with no dialog and no per-workspace consent, from the studio at the computer, a phone signed in over remote access, a scheduled task, a bot or `delorun headless`. Settings, Permissions shows a card with the date and a Turn off button, which also works from a remote studio, and a small "Dangerous mode" badge under the sidebar logo opens it. New chats still start on Workspace Write unless the workspace's default says otherwise.

Before an external agent such as Claude Code or Codex runs, Delorun asks you at the home's own computer, saying that it runs outside the sandbox, can reach your files and Delorun's home, and uses your own account. A phone signed in over remote access cannot answer.

"Allow for this workspace" on the approval card, or `delorun workspace external-agents <folder> <agent> on`, lets an agent start there without asking; Settings, External agents and `delorun workspace external-agents <folder> <agent> off` revoke it.

A read-only chat and a chat without a workspace folder never start an external agent, a run cannot start outside the chat's workspace, the question names the folder the agent runs in, and each run stops after 30 minutes. A full-access chat and `delorun headless` cannot ask, so they start an agent only where you allowed it for the workspace.
The model can no longer install or turn on an external-agent plugin, such as Claude Code, Codex or the ACP one, through plugin management.

Settings, External agents has its own switch, **Ask before external agents run**, on by default, and the run time limit, from 1 to 1440 minutes. Setup's prompts answer does not change either, and only the home's own computer can turn the question off.
A Privacy page in Settings states that Delo has no telemetry of its own and turns DeepSeek's session-log upload and desktop analytics on, after showing what each sends and where, or off again.

With setup's Dangerous answer on, the permission new chats start in and the external-agent consent that a phone loosened are set back when the mode ends, unless you changed them at your computer since.

A terminal opened or attached from a phone or browser always needs that device unlocked: setup's Dangerous answer, a full-access workspace and the old **Terminal from phone without unlock** switch no longer waive the unlock. The switch is gone from Settings, Devices; a home that still has it set keeps working and ignores the old setting. A phone with a terminal, or prompting a chat in a full-access workspace, has the computer's authority, so treat an unlocked phone as the computer.
A Delorun that keeps running for weeks now deletes expired log records itself, at the first hourly check after they are 14 days old, instead of waiting for you to run a `delorun` command.

Delorun's log now removes more of what it holds: the keys it loads from the credentials file, `.env` files and the environment, keys you set later from the studio or a phone, the studio's signing secret, session tokens, owner codes, pairing codes and the home key. Records of a chat's turn carry its session id and turn number, so `delorun logs --session` and `--turn` find them.

Delorun's log labels messages from upstream and other code it does not own as captured, because they can quote your chats. Delorun's log now also removes the elevation codes you type at the computer and the keys in your `.env` files, and it keeps a replaced or deleted provider key hidden, since the provider still accepts it until you revoke it.
DeepSeek's session-log upload and DeepSeek Harness's desktop analytics are off until you turn them on.

The threat model, the execution-vectors page, the contracts and the package READMEs now state only the protections the code provides, and where each applies: Delo's confinement, consents, fetch guard and privacy defaults apply to the profile that `delorun` and `delorun start` run, not to `delorun headless`, `delorun plugin` or the desktop app, and on Windows the sandbox confines writes only. Each contract page opens with what is built, and protections that are not built, such as reach, Docker workspaces, the plugin revocation list and most `delorun verify` checks, are described as design pages instead.

A chat never turns a plugin on at any protection level: with protection off, `undo` and `restore` in the plugin manager, and a turn-on whose `enabled` is not the boolean `false`, now wait for you at the computer, as an install already did.

Programs the agent starts no longer inherit a web address that carries a token, such as `https://<token>@host` or an error-reporting address with its key, or the variables that point at Kubernetes or Kerberos credentials, a MySQL password or a passphrase. An agent socket listed in `PATH` or a similar search list now drops only that entry, so the rest of `PATH` still reaches the program. An address that names only a user, such as `postgres://user@db/app`, is not passed on either, because a token in that place looks the same; pass such a value to the program explicitly.

A model-authored write to a skill, a preset, or a workspace's `AGENTS.md` asks for an approval that names the instruction-layer effect, because these instructions load in every future chat, and shows the diff, on every permission preset including full access. It also asks for a write through a linked folder or file, through a hard link to the file itself, for a differently capitalised name on a disk that ignores letter case, and for a write to the profile and home configuration files that hold presets.

An MCP server that would run as a local command is held until its command is accepted: the exact command with its arguments, its working folder and its environment variables, and the program and folder they lead to on this computer, with the command shell that runs a Windows `.cmd` file, are checked before the server starts. A command that has not been accepted keeps the server stopped and asks again; an accepted command starts that exact program without asking until any of these change, including the folder Delo runs in, its `PATH` or its `COMSPEC`. A `.env` file can no longer set `COMSPEC` or `PATHEXT`. The request names the environment variables without their values. The check holds whatever order the settings list the server and the consent in, and a command accepted by an earlier build is asked about again.

Approving a scheduled task names the recurrence it arms, the chat its deliveries reach and the permission preset that chat runs under, and a due delivery refuses, pausing the task, when that chat no longer runs the preset the task was approved under. The approval also names the task, the start of its message and the chat by its title, and for a new chat the folder it opens in and the preset that chat will really start with, such as its workspace's; the task is then held to the preset you were shown. Every occurrence is checked, a task that opens a new chat is checked before the chat exists, so a refused delivery leaves no empty chat behind, and a reminder still waiting from before a restart is checked again before it runs. When the check cannot give a clear answer, nothing is delivered: an answer it does not recognise refuses, and a check that fails keeps the task waiting and reports the failure instead of delivering.
A `.env` file in a folder you work in can no longer set `OPENSSL_CONF`, `GCONV_PATH`, `NODE_ICU_DATA`, `LD_*` or the other variables Delo's launcher removes before it starts the runtime.

`web_fetch` refuses to reach loopback, link-local, private-network, carrier-grade NAT (the range a tailnet and its API use), multicast and reserved addresses, and the address that names no destination at all, before it opens a connection. An IPv6 address that reaches an IPv4 address (mapped, compatible or translated for a network without IPv4) is judged as the IPv4 address it stands for.
Delo's profiles turn that protection on; a stock configuration keeps its old behaviour.
`web_fetch` connects only to the addresses it checked. A name that answers differently when the connection opens than when it was checked can no longer send the fetch to another address.

A chat can no longer use the plugin manager to switch off, reconfigure or remove Delo's consent and guard plugins, the update check or the sandbox, even under full access, so one chat cannot turn these protections off for every workspace. The Plugins page shows them as locked too; you change them by editing your profile's configuration.

In a task run with `delorun headless` with changes protection on, an agent's request to install, update or remove a plugin no longer runs: it waits in `delorun changes` for you to apply or discard it at your computer, as in the studio. Its first write to the folder of a plugin you approved asks for your approval, which nothing in a one-shot run can give, so the write is refused.

A task run with `delorun headless` now runs under Delo's guards, as the studio does. Web fetches of private, loopback and link-local addresses are refused, and a write to a skill, a preset or an `AGENTS.md`, a new stdio MCP server and a scheduled follow-up are refused, because nothing in a one-shot run can answer the approval they need. The task's model cannot turn these guards off through plugin management.

Full access in a headless task is refused unless you turned on full access for that folder, with `delorun workspace full-access <folder> on` or in the studio. A request for it with `--permission-mode` (`danger-full-access` or a preset of yours that selects it) or `DSH_PERMISSION_MODE=danger-full-access` is refused before anything starts, with a message that names the folder and the command that grants it; any other way of switching to full access during the task is refused by the same consent inside Delo.
DeepSeek's session-log upload is off by default in a headless task, as in the studio, and the feedback telemetry exporter is off.

The task starts only after Delo has checked that these protections are active. If the headless setup lost them, `delorun headless` stops and says how to restore them: remove `profiles/headless/delo-migrations.json` or the `profiles/headless` folder in your Delo home.
Delo refuses to use a home folder or secret file that other users on your computer could read, and prints the `chmod` command that fixes it.

Spilled tool output lives in the home's own `spill/` folder instead of the shared temporary folder, so the rule that keeps a confined command out of your home keeps it out of your spilled output too; the temporary folder is used only for a home that cannot hold it.

The home's `.env` file is read only when it is your own file, readable by you alone, and a real file rather than a link; one that is not stops the start with the exact command that fixes it (`chmod 600 <file>`), as the credentials file already does, so another local user cannot choose what your sessions load.
The anonymous id file is created readable by you alone, and the home directory the harness creates for it is private to you.

MCP servers can no longer use a stored credential to change what a reviewed start runs. A `${credential:NAME}` in a server's command, folder or a variable that changes what runs (`PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD`, `PYTHONPATH` and the like) is refused when the server loads, and an argument that is only a credential and would start with `-` is refused at start. The review shows templated arguments as written, with a note that they are filled from stored credentials.

An MCP server you allowed asks again before it starts if the program it runs, or a script file its arguments name, changed since you allowed it: Delorun remembers the contents of the program and of a file an argument names, such as the `server.js` of `node server.js`, the `./hook.js` of `--import=./hook.js` or the file a `node_modules/.bin` link points to. If one of them is rewritten or a link points elsewhere, Delorun asks you again before the server starts, at startup and also when the server restarts after it stopped, and shows "A file it runs changed since you allowed it". The server starts from the file the link pointed to when it was checked, under the name you configured, so a virtual environment's `python` still finds its virtual environment, and the review shows that file when the command is a link. Files the program loads by itself, such as other modules of a package, and code that `npx` or `uvx` downloads are not covered, so the review also names the folder and files of the server that your chats can write to.

The list of files a turn changed is now read without running any program that the repository's settings, attributes or hooks name, such as a file-system monitor, a filter or a hook, so a command the agent ran cannot plant one there to run later with your full access. The git commands that read it also run inside the chat's sandbox, with no more access than the agent's own commands, and a git older than 2.31 is no longer used for the list. Its working copies now live in your user cache folder, which the sandbox does not open to the agent's commands, instead of the temporary folder, and nothing is copied there while a workspace or extra folder of any chat contains it.

The sandbox keeps confined commands from reading or writing Delo's home and from connecting to the sockets of Delo's own services and of Docker, where the platform enforces it. A writable workspace that contains the home is refused for commands, and the file tools refuse to read, search or write inside it. A key file there stays out of reach of a command the agent runs.

Searching the machine with `glob` or `grep` no longer reaches Delo's home: a search over a folder that contains it lists none of the home's files and prints none of their matched lines, so a pattern or a word that matched a key file there finds nothing. The search runs in the same sandbox as the agent's commands, so a folder the agent swaps for a link to the home while a search runs shows nothing of it either, and where the sandbox cannot run, the search fails instead of running unprotected. A session under full access still searches everywhere it reaches.

Reading, editing, writing, creating or deleting a file with `read`, `read_image`, `str_replace_editor`, `edit`, `write` or `apply_patch` fails instead of reaching a file in Delo's home when a folder on its path is swapped for a link to the home between the check and the change.

Tool output too long for a chat is saved in Delo's home, where `read` and `grep` in that chat can open it as the chat's notice says, while other chats and the commands the agent runs cannot. When the home cannot hold it, the output stays in the chat rather than going to a temporary folder those commands could read.

The model can no longer offer you a file from Delo's home as a deliverable: presenting a file inside the home, or through a link that leads into it, is refused before the file is looked at, as opening it already was. A session under full access can still present any file it reaches.
The sandbox records which of these rules each platform cannot enforce: Linux cannot block socket connections, and Windows does not limit reads.

The Linux sandbox launcher refuses a grant path that names a symbolic link in any part and does not run the command, so a path swapped for a link after it was checked cannot widen what a command may touch.

Under WSL, a command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer start a Windows program through WSL's interop, by its path, by name or as a copy. Where the sandbox cannot use bubblewrap, its fallback cannot block this, so it refuses to run commands under WSL rather than leave this way out open.

Under WSL, and on any other virtual machine whose system offers it, a command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer open the virtual-machine connection to the host, which WSL's interop runs over. The sandbox also turns off io_uring for those commands, which could open that connection another way, so a program that needs io_uring fails there. A 32-bit program that opens network connections the old way cannot open any.

A command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer leave it through your session's services: it cannot start a program with `systemd-run --user` or through the session bus, reach the system bus, a tmux or screen server or the X server, or use your gpg-agent, keyring or the ssh-agent `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` names, because the sandbox hides their sockets. Where the sandbox cannot use bubblewrap, its fallback cannot hide them, so it refuses to run commands on a machine that has them rather than leave this way out open. A desktop's X server and a session bus started by `dbus-launch` can also listen on sockets no file names, which the sandbox does not hide.

A command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer reach Docker Desktop's control sockets under WSL or on Linux, through which it could change Docker Desktop's settings and act on containers, or the local control socket of Tailscale.

A read-only command the agent runs in the sandbox now sees an empty `/tmp`, apart from a workspace that lies in it, as a command that may write already did, so it can no longer reach the sockets other programs keep in `/tmp`. A `glob` or `grep` search rooted elsewhere in `/tmp` finds nothing. With bubblewrap, io_uring is now off for confined commands on any machine with these session services, not only under WSL.

A plugin's key, a setting the plugin marks as secret such as the DeepSeek API key of web search, is never saved into your profile's settings files, which the profile history keeps in git: saving one from Settings or through the agent is refused with where to put it instead, and the history saves no version that holds one, while it still lists your versions and undo and restore still work.

If a settings file already holds such a key, the next start moves it into the credentials file and points the plugin at it, telling you which file and setting changed and never showing the key; a key Delo cannot move, because the setting has no place to name a stored key, stays and every start tells you how to move it. If an earlier Delo already saved a key in the profile history, replace it with a new one.
A damaged or hostile session log can no longer expand a single compressed frame without a limit; a frame that would grow past 64 MiB is reported as corrupt instead of exhausting memory.
A session log that another process was migrating at the same time is accepted only when its contents decode to the same chat plus a valid append, not merely when its first bytes match.

`delorun setup` stores the model key through a new file that only you can read and that replaces the credentials file in one step, while it holds the same lock as the studio's own writes to that file; a left-over or planted temporary file never receives the key, and an interrupted write leaves the credentials file as it was.

A start now checks which plugin runs each protection, not only that a row with its name is on: a patch or a plugin that adds a second sandbox row or a second copy of one of Delo's guard rows under another plugin is refused, naming the file, safe mode never skips one of them, and once the studio has started each protection's service must come from its own plugin.
No chat turn in the studio reaches the model until the start has checked the running studio's protections; a turn sent before that waits, and is refused if the start is refused.
A `.env` file in the folder you run `delorun` from, or in Delo's home, can no longer set a `DELO_` setting such as the launcher's release roots; Delo refuses to start and names the file.

When the release you updated to fails its start check, only `delorun`, `delorun start` and `delorun recover rollback`, with nothing after `--`, start the release before it to roll back; any other command, `delorun verify` and `delorun stop` included, is refused with what failed and `delorun recover rollback` as the way back, and changes nothing.

An update checks again, right before it stops Delo for the switch, that no other profile's Delo or `delorun headless` started using your chats since it began, and stops without changing anything if one did.

The profile names `headless`, `data-users`, `node_modules` and `desktop`, and the Windows device names such as `con` and `nul`, are reserved: `delorun`, `delorun plugin`, `delorun logs`, the launcher and setup refuse them and say why, and `delorun plugin` and `delorun logs` refuse a command line that names two different profiles.
A Delo running in another container or sandbox that shares your home now counts as running, so its home lock is never taken over as if it had stopped.

Delo checks every start against the protections it promises before anything runs, and again once the studio has started: the sandbox protects Delo's home, Delo's consent and guard plugins are on, and your prompts answer is the one setup recorded. A patch, your home's own `cordis.patch.yml` included, that turns one of them off or points the sandbox at its own runner stops the start with the file to fix, or `delorun recover safe-mode` to start without your plugins.
`delorun headless` now runs its task under the same sandbox protection of Delo's home as the studio, and refuses `--profile`, `--patch` and `--from-default-profile`.

`delorun` refuses to start when your command-line profile cannot load Delo's own bundle, and prints how to fix it, instead of starting with DeepSeek Harness's defaults, which upload session logs to DeepSeek.
`delorun` stops and tells you how to fix it when one of Delo's own plugins, such as the Privacy section in Settings, fails to load, instead of running without it.

`delorun stop --now` now ends a Delo that does not answer or does not exit, with `SIGTERM` and then `SIGKILL`, but only after it confirms the process is the one holding the profile's lock; a process it cannot confirm is never signalled, and the command says which process to check. On Windows it never signals.

A start that Delo refuses after the studio has booted now stops that studio itself and always reports why with a non-zero exit, instead of letting the process end early, sometimes with code 0, before the refusal and the recovery of an interrupted update had run.

Refusals and unexpected failures are printed in the same what, why and what-you-can-do form with secrets such as API keys redacted, and an unexpected failure's full detail goes to the home process's log instead of a stack trace on the terminal.

`delorun recover rollback` with no Delo running now counts as the only user of your chats while it runs, so another profile's Delo cannot start in the middle of it; `delorun plugin` now counts as a user of your chats while it runs.
The record of Delo's one-time profile changes now lives with the profile, and an unreadable record makes Delo skip the changes and say so, so a change you undid is not made again.

A link that signs you in to the studio now works once and only for one minute, so a copy of it left in your terminal's scrollback, your shell history, your browser history or another program's command line can no longer be used to sign in after you have opened it. Run `delorun open` to open the studio in your browser at any time; `delorun open --print` prints a fresh link instead, for a computer without a browser or one you reach through an SSH port forward, and `--port` makes it for a forwarded port other than the studio's own. A link works only at the address it names, and opened at another address it says which one it was made for. Starting Delo prints the studio's address without a link, and an old link tells you to run `delorun open`.

With the fetch protection on, `web_fetch` judges an address written into the URL as an IPv6 literal, such as `http://[2001:db8::1]/`, like any other address: a public one is fetched, and a loopback or link-local one, such as `http://[::1]/` or `http://[fe80::1]/`, is refused. Every IPv6 literal had been refused, public ones included.

Your home folder itself, a filesystem root, the Delo home, DeepSeek Harness's `~/.dsh` home and any folder that contains one of them cannot be a workspace. The guide's folder chooser and the workspaces plugin refuse them and say why and what to choose instead.

Each workspace has a network setting for the commands the model runs in the sandbox: open, as before and by default; allowlist, where commands reach only the hosts you list, through an egress proxy that never looks up an unlisted name and refuses a listed name that points at a private, loopback or link-local address; or off, with no network at all. `web_fetch` follows the same setting. Choose it in Settings, Network, at the computer that runs Delo; a change that lets commands reach more asks you to confirm it.

An allowlist entry allows ports 80 and 443; write `host:port`, such as `github.com:22`, to allow another port. Under allowlist and off, commands also cannot reach the services that look names up or send traffic for them: systemd-resolved, nscd, avahi, the system D-Bus, snapd, CUPS and Tailscale's daemon. Other sockets stay reachable, such as an ssh connection you keep open or gpg's dirmngr under your home folder.

The setting holds on Linux with bubblewrap, WSL2 included. Where the sandbox cannot enforce it (Landlock alone, or any platform other than Linux), a workspace set to allowlist or off runs no commands instead of running them with your network.

A new guide page, "Prompt injection and data exfiltration", explains what each setting closes and what stays open whatever you choose: commands under full access, plugins and MCP servers, plugins the model writes, `web_search`, images and links in replies, files you share later, and a command that reaches a program outside the sandbox through a socket the sandbox does not hide, such as one in your home folder.
Feedback no longer goes to DeepSeek. Delo's studio hides the feedback buttons and the `/feedback` command, and it sends no session-log prefix to DeepSeek's feedback collector.

Remote access: `delorun reach on tailscale` lets you open the studio from your phone or another device over your own Tailscale tailnet, at `https://<computer>.<tailnet>.ts.net`. It is off until you turn it on, also from the remote access section of `delorun setup`'s Full mode, and `delorun reach off` turns it off. `delorun reach status` shows whether it is on and ready.

A device can open your chats only after you approve it at your computer: run `delorun devices approve` or choose Add a device in Settings → Devices, then type the 8-digit code the device shows. The device's sign-in page walks you through these steps in English or Chinese, light or dark, shows the code large with the time left, and says what to do next when approval is closed, the code expired or was cancelled, too many devices are waiting, the computer can't be reached, or the browser can't keep a sign-in key. `delorun devices list` lists approved devices, and `delorun devices remove` or Remove in Settings → Devices signs a device out at once.

An approved phone can do what you do at your computer with your chats and workspaces: read and reply to chats, start one in a workspace you have with any of your presets, read the files of its own workspace and its changes, see which plugins are installed, rename, pin, archive and reorder chats and workspaces, move a workspace to the trash, set goals, schedule follow-ups, choose the model, answer ordinary prompts and stop a run. A preset you choose on the phone decides the tools a chat runs with but grants no access by itself: a workspace's full access and every approval prompt are still answered at the computer. Credentials, your account, granting full access, and devices and remote access always stay at your computer. A remote session ends after 12 hours in which the phone sent nothing and 14 days after sign-in, and its open connections close then.

A few sensitive actions on a phone need a short unlock you approve at your computer: changing settings, running the slash commands that change only the chat (`/compact`, `/export`, `/goal`, `/permission` and `/plan`), installing or changing plugins other than Delo's own guards, opening a terminal, starting a chat in a folder that is not one of your workspaces and adding a workspace. The phone says the action needs a quick unlock and shows an 8-digit code; type it in Settings → Devices on your computer or with `delorun devices elevate`. While unlocked the phone shows until when, with Lock now; an unlock lasts 15 minutes, never extends, and ends early when you lock it on either side or the phone's session ends. Even unlocked, a phone cannot loosen the permission new chats start in, for example toward full access; it can still make it stricter.
`delorun reach on tailscale` refuses while Tailscale Funnel is on for the address, and Delorun stops serving if Funnel is turned on later.

A phone signed in to Tailscale as the same user as your computer can now ask to pair without an approval window. The studio at your computer shows the request with **Enter code** and **Decline**; you type the 8-digit code the phone shows, as before, and the code is still required. `delorun setup reach` lets any device on your tailnet ask instead, and `delorun reach status` says who may ask. The `pairing` settings in the `@delo/home-auth` row also set how the request is shown, the approval window and request lifetimes, and how many requests one Tailscale user may have waiting.
