Programs the agent starts no longer inherit a web address that carries a token, such as `https://<token>@host` or an error-reporting address with its key, or the variables that point at Kubernetes or Kerberos credentials, a MySQL password or a passphrase. An agent socket listed in `PATH` or a similar search list now drops only that entry, so the rest of `PATH` still reaches the program. An address that names only a user, such as `postgres://user@db/app`, is not passed on either, because a token in that place looks the same; pass such a value to the program explicitly.

A model-authored write to a skill, a preset, or a workspace's `AGENTS.md` asks for an approval that names the instruction-layer effect, because these instructions load in every future chat, and shows the diff, on every permission preset including full access. It also asks for a write through a linked folder or file, through a hard link to the file itself, for a differently capitalised name on a disk that ignores letter case, and for a write to the profile and home configuration files that hold presets.

An MCP server that would run as a local command is held until its command is accepted: the exact command with its arguments, its working folder and its environment variables, and the program and folder they lead to on this computer, with the command shell that runs a Windows `.cmd` file, are checked before the server starts. A command that has not been accepted keeps the server stopped and asks again; an accepted command starts that exact program without asking until any of these change, including the folder Delo runs in, its `PATH` or its `COMSPEC`. A `.env` file can no longer set `COMSPEC` or `PATHEXT`. The request names the environment variables without their values. The check holds whatever order the settings list the server and the consent in, and a command accepted by an earlier build is asked about again.

Approving a scheduled task names the recurrence it arms, the chat its deliveries reach and the permission preset that chat runs under, and a due delivery refuses, pausing the task, when that chat no longer runs the preset the task was approved under. The approval also names the task, the start of its message and the chat by its title, and for a new chat the folder it opens in and the preset that chat will really start with, such as its workspace's; the task is then held to the preset you were shown. Every occurrence is checked, a task that opens a new chat is checked before the chat exists, so a refused delivery leaves no empty chat behind, and a reminder still waiting from before a restart is checked again before it runs. When the check cannot give a clear answer, nothing is delivered: an answer it does not recognise refuses, and a check that fails keeps the task waiting and reports the failure instead of delivering.
A `.env` file in a folder you work in can no longer set `OPENSSL_CONF`, `GCONV_PATH`, `NODE_ICU_DATA`, `LD_*` or the other variables Delo's launcher removes before it starts the runtime.

`web_fetch` refuses to reach loopback, link-local, private-network, carrier-grade NAT (the range a tailnet and its API use), multicast and reserved addresses, and the address that names no destination at all, before it opens a connection. An IPv6 address that reaches an IPv4 address (mapped, compatible or translated for a network without IPv4) is judged as the IPv4 address it stands for.
Delo's profiles turn that protection on; a stock configuration keeps its old behaviour.
`web_fetch` connects only to the addresses it checked. A name that answers differently when the connection opens than when it was checked can no longer send the fetch to another address.

A chat can no longer use the plugin manager to switch off, reconfigure or remove Delo's consent and guard plugins, the update check or the sandbox, even under full access, so one chat cannot turn these protections off for every workspace. The Plugins page shows them as locked too; you change them by editing your profile's configuration.

In a task run with `delorun headless` with changes protection on, an agent's request to install, update or remove a plugin no longer runs: it waits in `delorun changes` for you to apply or discard it at your computer, as in the studio. Its first write to the folder of a plugin you approved asks for your approval, which nothing in a one-shot run can give, so the write is refused.

A task run with `delorun headless` now runs under Delo's guards, as the studio does. Web fetches of private, loopback and link-local addresses are refused, and a write to a skill, a preset or an `AGENTS.md`, a new stdio MCP server and a scheduled follow-up are refused, because nothing in a one-shot run can answer the approval they need. The task's model cannot turn these guards off through plugin management.

Full access in a headless task is refused unless you turned on full access for that folder, with `delorun workspace full-access <folder> on` or in the studio. A request for it with `--permission-mode` (`danger-full-access` or a preset of yours that selects it) or `DSH_PERMISSION_MODE=danger-full-access` is refused before anything starts, with a message that names the folder and the command that grants it; any other way of switching to full access during the task is refused by the same consent inside Delo.
DeepSeek's session-log upload is off by default in a headless task, as in the studio, and the feedback telemetry exporter is off.

The task starts only after Delo has checked that these protections are active. If the headless setup lost them, `delorun headless` stops and says how to restore them: remove `profiles/headless/delo-migrations.json` or the `profiles/headless` folder in your Delo home.
Delo refuses to use a home folder or secret file that other users on your computer could read, and prints the `chmod` command that fixes it.

Spilled tool output lives in the home's own `spill/` folder instead of the shared temporary folder, so the rule that keeps a confined command out of your home keeps it out of your spilled output too; the temporary folder is used only for a home that cannot hold it.

The home's `.env` file is read only when it is your own file, readable by you alone, and a real file rather than a link; one that is not stops the start with the exact command that fixes it (`chmod 600 <file>`), as the credentials file already does, so another local user cannot choose what your sessions load.
The anonymous id file is created readable by you alone, and the home directory the harness creates for it is private to you.

MCP servers can no longer use a stored credential to change what a reviewed start runs. A `${credential:NAME}` in a server's command, folder or a variable that changes what runs (`PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD`, `PYTHONPATH` and the like) is refused when the server loads, and an argument that is only a credential and would start with `-` is refused at start. The review shows templated arguments as written, with a note that they are filled from stored credentials.

An MCP server you allowed asks again before it starts if the program it runs, or a script file its arguments name, changed since you allowed it: Delorun remembers the contents of the program and of a file an argument names, such as the `server.js` of `node server.js`, the `./hook.js` of `--import=./hook.js` or the file a `node_modules/.bin` link points to. If one of them is rewritten or a link points elsewhere, Delorun asks you again before the server starts, at startup and also when the server restarts after it stopped, and shows "A file it runs changed since you allowed it". The server starts from the file the link pointed to when it was checked, under the name you configured, so a virtual environment's `python` still finds its virtual environment, and the review shows that file when the command is a link. Files the program loads by itself, such as other modules of a package, and code that `npx` or `uvx` downloads are not covered, so the review also names the folder and files of the server that your chats can write to.

The list of files a turn changed is now read without running any program that the repository's settings, attributes or hooks name, such as a file-system monitor, a filter or a hook, so a command the agent ran cannot plant one there to run later with your full access. The git commands that read it also run inside the chat's sandbox, with no more access than the agent's own commands, and a git older than 2.31 is no longer used for the list. Its working copies now live in your user cache folder, which the sandbox does not open to the agent's commands, instead of the temporary folder, and nothing is copied there while a workspace or extra folder of any chat contains it.

The sandbox keeps confined commands from reading or writing Delo's home and from connecting to the sockets of Delo's own services and of Docker, where the platform enforces it. A writable workspace that contains the home is refused for commands, and the file tools refuse to read, search or write inside it. A key file there stays out of reach of a command the agent runs.

Searching the machine with `glob` or `grep` no longer reaches Delo's home: a search over a folder that contains it lists none of the home's files and prints none of their matched lines, so a pattern or a word that matched a key file there finds nothing. The search runs in the same sandbox as the agent's commands, so a folder the agent swaps for a link to the home while a search runs shows nothing of it either, and where the sandbox cannot run, the search fails instead of running unprotected. A session under full access still searches everywhere it reaches.

Reading, editing, writing, creating or deleting a file with `read`, `read_image`, `str_replace_editor`, `edit`, `write` or `apply_patch` fails instead of reaching a file in Delo's home when a folder on its path is swapped for a link to the home between the check and the change.

Tool output too long for a chat is saved in Delo's home, where `read` and `grep` in that chat can open it as the chat's notice says, while other chats and the commands the agent runs cannot. When the home cannot hold it, the output stays in the chat rather than going to a temporary folder those commands could read.

The model can no longer offer you a file from Delo's home as a deliverable: presenting a file inside the home, or through a link that leads into it, is refused before the file is looked at, as opening it already was. A session under full access can still present any file it reaches.
The sandbox records which of these rules each platform cannot enforce: Linux cannot block socket connections, and Windows does not limit reads.

The Linux sandbox launcher refuses a grant path that names a symbolic link in any part and does not run the command, so a path swapped for a link after it was checked cannot widen what a command may touch.

Under WSL, a command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer start a Windows program through WSL's interop, by its path, by name or as a copy. Where the sandbox cannot use bubblewrap, its fallback cannot block this, so it refuses to run commands under WSL rather than leave this way out open.

Under WSL, and on any other virtual machine whose system offers it, a command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer open the virtual-machine connection to the host, which WSL's interop runs over. The sandbox also turns off io_uring for those commands, which could open that connection another way, so a program that needs io_uring fails there. A 32-bit program that opens network connections the old way cannot open any.

A command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer leave it through your session's services: it cannot start a program with `systemd-run --user` or through the session bus, reach the system bus, a tmux or screen server or the X server, or use your gpg-agent, keyring or the ssh-agent `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` names, because the sandbox hides their sockets. Where the sandbox cannot use bubblewrap, its fallback cannot hide them, so it refuses to run commands on a machine that has them rather than leave this way out open. A desktop's X server and a session bus started by `dbus-launch` can also listen on sockets no file names, which the sandbox does not hide.

A command the agent runs in the sandbox can no longer reach Docker Desktop's control sockets under WSL or on Linux, through which it could change Docker Desktop's settings and act on containers, or the local control socket of Tailscale.

A read-only command the agent runs in the sandbox now sees an empty `/tmp`, apart from a workspace that lies in it, as a command that may write already did, so it can no longer reach the sockets other programs keep in `/tmp`. A `glob` or `grep` search rooted elsewhere in `/tmp` finds nothing. With bubblewrap, io_uring is now off for confined commands on any machine with these session services, not only under WSL.

A plugin's key, a setting the plugin marks as secret such as the DeepSeek API key of web search, is never saved into your profile's settings files, which the profile history keeps in git: saving one from Settings or through the agent is refused with where to put it instead, and the history saves no version that holds one, while it still lists your versions and undo and restore still work.

If a settings file already holds such a key, the next start moves it into the credentials file and points the plugin at it, telling you which file and setting changed and never showing the key; a key Delo cannot move, because the setting has no place to name a stored key, stays and every start tells you how to move it. If an earlier Delo already saved a key in the profile history, replace it with a new one.
A damaged or hostile session log can no longer expand a single compressed frame without a limit; a frame that would grow past 64 MiB is reported as corrupt instead of exhausting memory.
A session log that another process was migrating at the same time is accepted only when its contents decode to the same chat plus a valid append, not merely when its first bytes match.

`delorun setup` stores the model key through a new file that only you can read and that replaces the credentials file in one step, while it holds the same lock as the studio's own writes to that file; a left-over or planted temporary file never receives the key, and an interrupted write leaves the credentials file as it was.

A start now checks which plugin runs each protection, not only that a row with its name is on: a patch or a plugin that adds a second sandbox row or a second copy of one of Delo's guard rows under another plugin is refused, naming the file, safe mode never skips one of them, and once the studio has started each protection's service must come from its own plugin.
No chat turn in the studio reaches the model until the start has checked the running studio's protections; a turn sent before that waits, and is refused if the start is refused.
A `.env` file in the folder you run `delorun` from, or in Delo's home, can no longer set a `DELO_` setting such as the launcher's release roots; Delo refuses to start and names the file.

When the release you updated to fails its start check, only `delorun`, `delorun start` and `delorun recover rollback`, with nothing after `--`, start the release before it to roll back; any other command, `delorun verify` and `delorun stop` included, is refused with what failed and `delorun recover rollback` as the way back, and changes nothing.

An update checks again, right before it stops Delo for the switch, that no other profile's Delo or `delorun headless` started using your chats since it began, and stops without changing anything if one did.

The profile names `headless`, `data-users`, `node_modules` and `desktop`, and the Windows device names such as `con` and `nul`, are reserved: `delorun`, `delorun plugin`, `delorun logs`, the launcher and setup refuse them and say why, and `delorun plugin` and `delorun logs` refuse a command line that names two different profiles.
A Delo running in another container or sandbox that shares your home now counts as running, so its home lock is never taken over as if it had stopped.

Delo checks every start against the protections it promises before anything runs, and again once the studio has started: the sandbox protects Delo's home, Delo's consent and guard plugins are on, and your prompts answer is the one setup recorded. A patch, your home's own `cordis.patch.yml` included, that turns one of them off or points the sandbox at its own runner stops the start with the file to fix, or `delorun recover safe-mode` to start without your plugins.
`delorun headless` now runs its task under the same sandbox protection of Delo's home as the studio, and refuses `--profile`, `--patch` and `--from-default-profile`.

`delorun` refuses to start when your command-line profile cannot load Delo's own bundle, and prints how to fix it, instead of starting with DeepSeek Harness's defaults, which upload session logs to DeepSeek.
`delorun` stops and tells you how to fix it when one of Delo's own plugins, such as the Privacy section in Settings, fails to load, instead of running without it.

`delorun stop --now` now ends a Delo that does not answer or does not exit, with `SIGTERM` and then `SIGKILL`, but only after it confirms the process is the one holding the profile's lock; a process it cannot confirm is never signalled, and the command says which process to check. On Windows it never signals.

A start that Delo refuses after the studio has booted now stops that studio itself and always reports why with a non-zero exit, instead of letting the process end early, sometimes with code 0, before the refusal and the recovery of an interrupted update had run.

Refusals and unexpected failures are printed in the same what, why and what-you-can-do form with secrets such as API keys redacted, and an unexpected failure's full detail goes to the home process's log instead of a stack trace on the terminal.

`delorun recover rollback` with no Delo running now counts as the only user of your chats while it runs, so another profile's Delo cannot start in the middle of it; `delorun plugin` now counts as a user of your chats while it runs.
The record of Delo's one-time profile changes now lives with the profile, and an unreadable record makes Delo skip the changes and say so, so a change you undid is not made again.

A link that signs you in to the studio now works once and only for one minute, so a copy of it left in your terminal's scrollback, your shell history, your browser history or another program's command line can no longer be used to sign in after you have opened it. Run `delorun open` to open the studio in your browser at any time; `delorun open --print` prints a fresh link instead, for a computer without a browser or one you reach through an SSH port forward, and `--port` makes it for a forwarded port other than the studio's own. A link works only at the address it names, and opened at another address it says which one it was made for. Starting Delo prints the studio's address without a link, and an old link tells you to run `delorun open`.

With the fetch protection on, `web_fetch` judges an address written into the URL as an IPv6 literal, such as `http://[2001:db8::1]/`, like any other address: a public one is fetched, and a loopback or link-local one, such as `http://[::1]/` or `http://[fe80::1]/`, is refused. Every IPv6 literal had been refused, public ones included.

Your home folder itself, a filesystem root, the Delo home, DeepSeek Harness's `~/.dsh` home and any folder that contains one of them cannot be a workspace. The guide's folder chooser and the workspaces plugin refuse them and say why and what to choose instead.

Each workspace has a network setting for the commands the model runs in the sandbox: open, as before and by default; allowlist, where commands reach only the hosts you list, through an egress proxy that never looks up an unlisted name and refuses a listed name that points at a private, loopback or link-local address; or off, with no network at all. `web_fetch` follows the same setting. Choose it in Settings, Network, at the computer that runs Delo; a change that lets commands reach more asks you to confirm it.

An allowlist entry allows ports 80 and 443; write `host:port`, such as `github.com:22`, to allow another port. Under allowlist and off, commands also cannot reach the services that look names up or send traffic for them: systemd-resolved, nscd, avahi, the system D-Bus, snapd, CUPS and Tailscale's daemon. Other sockets stay reachable, such as an ssh connection you keep open or gpg's dirmngr under your home folder.

The setting holds on Linux with bubblewrap, WSL2 included. Where the sandbox cannot enforce it (Landlock alone, or any platform other than Linux), a workspace set to allowlist or off runs no commands instead of running them with your network.

A new guide page, "Prompt injection and data exfiltration", explains what each setting closes and what stays open whatever you choose: commands under full access, plugins and MCP servers, plugins the model writes, `web_search`, images and links in replies, files you share later, and a command that reaches a program outside the sandbox through a socket the sandbox does not hide, such as one in your home folder.
Feedback no longer goes to DeepSeek. Delo's studio hides the feedback buttons and the `/feedback` command, and it sends no session-log prefix to DeepSeek's feedback collector.

Remote access: `delorun reach on tailscale` lets you open the studio from your phone or another device over your own Tailscale tailnet, at `https://<computer>.<tailnet>.ts.net`. It is off until you turn it on, also from the remote access section of `delorun setup`'s Full mode, and `delorun reach off` turns it off. `delorun reach status` shows whether it is on and ready.

A device can open your chats only after you approve it at your computer: run `delorun devices approve` or choose Add a device in Settings → Devices, then type the 8-digit code the device shows. The device's sign-in page walks you through these steps in English or Chinese, light or dark, shows the code large with the time left, and says what to do next when approval is closed, the code expired or was cancelled, too many devices are waiting, the computer can't be reached, or the browser can't keep a sign-in key. `delorun devices list` lists approved devices, and `delorun devices remove` or Remove in Settings → Devices signs a device out at once.

An approved phone can do what you do at your computer with your chats and workspaces: read and reply to chats, start one in a workspace you have with any of your presets, read the files of its own workspace and its changes, see which plugins are installed, rename, pin, archive and reorder chats and workspaces, move a workspace to the trash, set goals, schedule follow-ups, choose the model, answer ordinary prompts and stop a run. A preset you choose on the phone decides the tools a chat runs with but grants no access by itself: a workspace's full access and every approval prompt are still answered at the computer. Credentials, your account, granting full access, and devices and remote access always stay at your computer. A remote session ends after 12 hours in which the phone sent nothing and 14 days after sign-in, and its open connections close then.

A few sensitive actions on a phone need a short unlock you approve at your computer: changing settings, running the slash commands that change only the chat (`/compact`, `/export`, `/goal`, `/permission` and `/plan`), installing or changing plugins other than Delo's own guards, opening a terminal, starting a chat in a folder that is not one of your workspaces and adding a workspace. The phone says the action needs a quick unlock and shows an 8-digit code; type it in Settings → Devices on your computer or with `delorun devices elevate`. While unlocked the phone shows until when, with Lock now; an unlock lasts 15 minutes, never extends, and ends early when you lock it on either side or the phone's session ends. Even unlocked, a phone cannot loosen the permission new chats start in, for example toward full access; it can still make it stricter.
`delorun reach on tailscale` refuses while Tailscale Funnel is on for the address, and Delorun stops serving if Funnel is turned on later.

A phone signed in to Tailscale as the same user as your computer can now ask to pair without an approval window. The studio at your computer shows the request with **Enter code** and **Decline**; you type the 8-digit code the phone shows, as before, and the code is still required. `delorun setup reach` lets any device on your tailnet ask instead, and `delorun reach status` says who may ask. The `pairing` settings in the `@delo/home-auth` row also set how the request is shown, the approval window and request lifetimes, and how many requests one Tailscale user may have waiting. Settings → Devices shows and changes these choices at your computer.
Turning remote access on or off applies to the Delo that is running, which says whether the address is ready instead of asking you to restart; `delorun reach status` shows the live state.
`delorun reach on` checks that your Tailscale user may serve before it turns anything on, and names the one command to run when it may not.
`delorun start --background` starts Delo detached from the terminal whatever setup answered, and a start that stays in the terminal says how to run it in the background next time.

`delorun reach on tailscale` asks "This changes Tailscale on this computer … Continue? (y/N)" in a terminal before it changes anything. `--yes` skips the question. Without a terminal and without `--yes` it changes nothing and says to add `--yes`.
Opening your remote address, or a page of it, on a device that is not signed in takes you to the sign-in page instead of showing an error, and back to that page once you sign in.
A device reads only the files whose real location lies inside its chat's workspace: a link inside the workspace that leads elsewhere, and Delo's own folder, are refused.

A plugin you link from a folder runs from a copy of its content kept in the Delo home. With protection on, edits in the folder wait for your review and break nothing that is running; with protection off, the default, they load without review and are recorded. Plugins linked before this release are approved as they are at the first start, which says so once.

Changes protection is off by default, so you change your harness freely: a plugin you link from a folder loads your saved edits at each start and, while Delo runs, each time you save a file in its folder, without a work session. Each load is recorded as a change that loaded without review, which `delorun changes list` shows and `delorun changes undo` takes back, and content you undid does not load again until you save something else. A saved version that fails to load goes back to what ran before and is not tried again until you save again. `delorun changes protection on` makes changes wait for your review instead, and takes effect without a restart.

A composition can forbid embedded code in its own patch files: with `refuseCode` on, loading refuses `!!js` expressions and patch `insert` rows and fails with an error naming the file and where the code sits. The switch is off, which changes nothing.

Settings, Plugins has Create a plugin: name a plugin, choose what it adds and a workspace, and Delo writes the starting files into the workspace's `plugins` folder, the same files `delorun plugin new` writes. Turn on lists the plugin in Changes for your review at the computer, also in dangerous mode; a phone or another device is told to do this at your computer.

Ask the agent in a chat for a plugin and it makes one in the chat's workspace, under `plugins/<name>`, with the new `delo-plugin-authoring` skill. It cannot turn the plugin on, at any protection level and in any chat access; that stays your step at the computer. Once the plugin is on, later edits to its files wait for your review when changes protection is on, and reload live, logged as loaded without review, when it is off, the default.
The Changes and instruction-consent plugins load when Delo runs its TypeScript sources directly; they failed to import and left the studio without Changes.

Installing a plugin checks it and every package it brings before any of its files are fetched or any install script runs: a package without an integrity hash, a git source not pinned to a full commit, a registry or download URL that is plain http, a known GitHub advisory, a version published in the last 24 hours and a name close to one you already have are each shown where you install it, on the Plugins page and in `delorun plugin`'s output. A known critical advisory stops the installation until you choose to install it anyway, with "Install anyway" or `--allow-advisory <id>`; everything else only warns. When the advisory or publish-time lookup cannot run, you are told so. Scopes and git owners you trust can be listed so their plugins show only critical advisories; linked and local plugin folders are not checked.

Delo records every file of each plugin it installs, checks them at every start and fully in `delorun verify`, and warns when a plugin changed since it was installed. Installed plugins get their own copies of their files, so an edit to pnpm's shared store no longer reaches them.

Plugins no longer fall back to the npmmirror registry unless you turn it on, in Settings → Privacy or with `delorun plugin mirror on`, and a package installed under the name of one of Delo's own components cannot stand in for it.

`delorun changes` lists the changes to your plugins, those that loaded without review and those that wait for your review, and shows each with its files, a diff and a summary of what it can do. `apply`, `discard` and `undo` decide about one change after you confirm in a terminal, with a second confirmation when the change runs commands, opens network connections or does anything else the summary names. A running Delo loads an applied change at once and goes back to what ran before when it fails to load. `off` and `on` turn one plugin off and on again, and `protection on` makes changes wait for your review, which `protection off`, the default, ends; each says what it means, asks, and applies without a restart. `work <plugin> [--for <minutes>]` loads every edit you save in a plugin's folder live for up to two hours, or the minutes you give up to eight hours, going back to the last version that loaded when an edit fails to load. `done <plugin>` shows the folder's version with its files and diff and approves exactly that version as one change; a session that ends without you, when Delo stops or its time is up, approves nothing and leaves the folder's content waiting for your review. `delorun status` names an open work session and when it ends. With protection on, a plugin you link with `delorun plugin --profile default add link:<folder>`, or bring back with a restore or undo, loads nothing from its folder until you apply its content, also while Delo runs; the approved copy includes the plugin's installed packages; and a plugin folder Delo cannot read no longer stops Delo from starting. When Delo fails to start right after you applied a change to a plugin or turned one on, it starts once more without that change, names it with `delorun changes apply <id>` and `undo <id>` at every start, in `delorun changes list` and in `delorun doctor`, and rewrites none of your files; when it fails again it points to `delorun recover safe-mode`.

Every `delorun` command answers `--help` (and `-h`, and `delorun help <command>`) with a short usage, its options and its exit codes, and exits 0 without starting anything. A wrong option now says which option and points to `delorun <command> --help`, and `delorun help` ends with a short list of the words the commands use: home, profile, studio, workspace, full access and reach.

`delorun start` starts Delo in the background, so you can close the terminal, and waits until it is running; `delorun start --foreground` runs it in your terminal. `delorun start --patch <file>` applies a patch file over your profile for that start only, as `dsh --patch` does, and Delo's own checks still apply to it; `--inspect` lets a debugger attach to Delo while you work on a plugin, after you confirm, since any process on the computer, the agent's sandboxed commands included, can then run code as Delo; `--inspect --yes` confirms without a terminal, safe mode refuses it, and `delorun status` shows it while it is open. `delorun` on its own does the same and opens the studio, then prints the studio's address and how to see, follow and stop Delo; if you chose during setup not to run Delo in the background, or pass `--foreground`, it runs in your terminal.
`delorun stop` stops Delo once running chats end, or at once with `--now`.
`delorun status` shows the home and profile in use, whether Delo is running, its process, runtime version and running chats, or prints them as JSON with `--json`.

`delorun plugin` and `delorun headless` work as their `dsh` counterparts do, inside your Delo home; an installed Delo runs plugin operations with the pnpm it carries, so you do not need pnpm on your computer. `delorun plugin` works on your Delo profile without `--profile`. When pnpm refuses to run a package's build, as it does for a plugin installed from git, `delorun plugin` asks whether to allow that one package's build and tries again; `--allow-build <name>` allows it without asking, and nothing allows every build at once.

When a `delorun` command or the launcher stops on a failure, it says what Delo did, why, with the error's code and the file or detail concerned, and what you can do next, naming your `--profile`; it never prints a stack trace.

`delorun workspace full-access <folder> on` turns on full access for a folder after showing what it means and asking you to confirm at a terminal; `off` turns it off, and without a folder the command lists the folders with full access. Every running studio counts the change within a second, whichever profile it runs, and after `off` the command names the profiles where Delo runs; a change made at the same moment by a studio is never lost. `delorun headless` in that folder can then run with full access.

`delorun mcp list` shows the local MCP servers Delo is holding, what changed since you allowed each (a new server; its command, arguments, working directory or environment variables changed, naming the variables that changed; its command or folder now points to a different file or folder on this computer; the acceptance list could not be read; or, for a server you allowed before Delo remembered each server separately, a one-time review) the exact file that runs and the folder it runs in (on Windows also the command shell that runs a `.cmd` or `.bat` file), and why it waits, and whether you declined or revoked it, then the servers you allowed and when you allowed each. Each server is allowed on its own, so two servers started with `npx` never share an answer. Values of environment variables stay hidden, except for the ones that change what runs, such as `PATH` and `NODE_OPTIONS`. `delorun mcp accept <server>` shows the server's command and starts it after you confirm at a terminal, and `delorun mcp decline <server>` keeps it stopped until its command or settings change.

`delorun mcp revoke <server>` shows an allowed server, and after you confirm at a terminal withdraws it and stops it; it stays stopped until its command or settings change or you accept it again, and your other servers stay allowed.

`delorun doctor` checks Docker, the format of the key of the provider new chats start on, the Delo home's permissions and whether the studio's port is free, and says whether the running release was checked against the release log: verified, refused, or unchecked with how long it has been and why, and what the last check for a newer release found. It sends nothing to the provider and starts no container.
`delorun doctor` checks the port the profile's studio uses, and a port held by this home's own Delo is reported as in use by Delo, not as a failure.

On Linux, `delorun doctor` checks whether bubblewrap can sandbox commands. Where it cannot, every sandboxed command is refused on a machine with a login session; the line says why, and where Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces blocks it, points to how to allow bubblewrap alone.
`delorun doctor` accepts a studio port of 0, which asks the system for a free port at each start, and prints no YAML warning for a profile that holds a `!!js` expression.

`delorun doctor` checks Docker, the DeepSeek API key's format, the Delo home's permissions and whether the studio's port is free, and says whether the running release was checked against the release log: verified, refused, or unchecked with how long it has been and why, and what the last check for a newer release found. It sends nothing to DeepSeek and starts no container.

`delorun doctor` checks your plugins: it lists what is installed in your profile, where each plugin came from and whether it is turned on, and warns or fails when a plugin needs another Delo or DeepSeek Harness version, is hidden by a plugin Delo ships under the same name, is turned on but not installed, did not load at the last start, or is left out because Delo is in safe mode. It reads files only and runs no plugin code.

Delo's own processes keep operational logs at fixed locations under your Delo home. Every record is redacted before it is written, so keys, tokens and cookie values Delo loads never reach a log; logs rotate at 10 MiB, keep 5 files, and are deleted 14 days after they were written while Delo runs. Your chats' session logs are not touched.
`delorun logs` lists every log's location and shows a log's recent records, filtered by chat, turn or age, follows new records, prints the stored JSON, and clears or prunes logs on request.

`delorun plugin` asks before it runs a build pnpm refused, such as the `prepare` script of a plugin installed from git, or takes `--allow-build <name>` for one package. The question starts on no, and nothing allows every build. With Delo's install check on, only the installation runs again, on the lockfile the check read; a lockfile that differs from it is refused and the profile put back.

`delorun plugin dev <folder>` links a plugin you are writing into your profile and keeps the running studio loading its latest code each time you save, building it first when it has a build script, until you press Ctrl+C; the plugin stays installed afterwards.

`delorun plugin new <name>` creates a plugin folder that builds and installs on the running release: a tool for the agent, an agent preset, a page in the studio's Settings, or a bundle that changes other plugins' settings, chosen with `--kind`. It prints the next commands: build the plugin, check it with `delorun plugin check`, and add it to your profile.

`delorun recover` shows where your profile stands and offers the way back: roll back to the last saved snapshot of the profile, or restore any earlier saved version. Both list the plugins, build approvals and version exemptions they bring back before anything is written, and a plugin version that has been revoked comes back turned off, with the reason shown.

`delorun recover --safe-mode` makes the next start leave out the third-party bundles and the rows that load them, so a plugin that cannot start no longer keeps the home from opening. The profile itself is untouched, with every row, setting and ejected plugin still there, and `delorun recover --exit-safe-mode` loads all of it again.

A restore or a rollback keeps Delo's own records in the profile, its version exemptions, its safety record and the last update report, when the saved version does not hold them, instead of removing them. It waits for the plugin manager while that is changing the profile, and refuses with nothing changed if the manager does not finish within two minutes.

Under WSL, `delorun open` and `delorun start --open` hand the studio's link to the browser `BROWSER` names when it is set, and to the Windows default browser only when it is not; `delorun open --print` prints the link and opens nothing.

`delorun verify` lists what this Delo runs: the release's version, commit and digests, the trusted root and its key, the launcher that started it, when every runtime file was last hashed and what the start check did, the plugins with where each came from, your changes, the rows your patch layers add with their `!!js` count, the skill folders including `~/.agents`, and the MCP servers. `--json` carries the same list under `bill`. A part Delo cannot check yet says so instead of reading as a pass.

The messages `delorun setup` prints, the studio's starter prompts and the chat refusals use British English, such as "catalogue", "summarise" and "organise", and a check keeps American spellings out of Delorun's own text.

Command output says "Delorun", not "Delo", in sentences and drops internal labels: `delorun logs` heads its list "Logs under …" and no longer lists a relay you may not run, `delorun verify` lists the checks it runs and says in one line how many more Delorun does not include, and `delorun reach status` says whether remote access is on or off and how to turn it on.

`delorun status` prints whether Delorun is running, the studio address, the version and the running chats. The process id, the start id, the home folder and the profile appear with `--verbose`, and `--json` still carries them.

`delorun start` that fails says "Delorun did not start", points to `delorun logs` and `delorun doctor`, and when another program holds the studio's port it says so and offers `delorun setup profile` or port 0. `delorun import-home` without a DeepSeek Harness folder says there is none and offers `--from`. `delorun workspace` with no action says to choose full-access or external-agents.
`delorun devices approve` and `delorun devices elevate` stop at once, with a message, when they have no terminal to type the code in, instead of waiting for five minutes.
`delorun --version` prints "Delorun" on its first line, and `delorun setup` and the default workspace's message name Delorun too.

`delorun plugin list` on a new profile says "No plugins added to the profile default." instead of printing nothing, `delorun plugin` on a profile that does not exist yet says "delorun: initialized profile …" where it said "dsh: …", and `delorun plugin` with no arguments shows Delorun's usage, not pnpm's message. Its other lines also say "delorun:" where they said "dsh:": warnings, the failed-command line and the rejected-installation lines, and the hints name `delorun plugin allow-version`, the command that grants the exemption. <!-- us-spelling: quoted output -->
`delorun open --print` and other output piped into a reader that stops early, such as `head -1`, ends quietly with exit 0 instead of reporting "write EPIPE".

Each `delorun` command now loads only the code it needs, so `delorun --version` and `delorun --help` answer in a fraction of the time they took, and `status`, `logs`, `trash` and the other short commands start sooner too. What the commands print and the exit codes are the same.
`delorun recover` takes its action as a word: `status`, `rollback`, `restore <version>`, `safe-mode` and `exit-safe-mode` replace `--rollback`, `--restore`, `--safe-mode` and `--exit-safe-mode`.
`delorun stop` and updates now wait for chats that are still answering.

Every `delorun` command starts about 9 seconds sooner: on a full-size runtime the launcher's check takes under a second instead of about ten, because it compares each file with what it recorded after the file was last hashed, and hashes only the files that changed since. It still hashes every file at install, on `delorun verify`, and at least every 7 days; `DELO_RUNTIME_FULL_CHECK_DAYS` sets that interval from 0, every start, to 30 days. Disk corruption that leaves a file's metadata alone is found by that full check, not by the next start. On macOS, Windows, overlay file systems such as a container's, and network or other file systems whose timestamps the computer does not set itself, every start still hashes every file.

An update no longer reads every file of a runtime again: it hashes the new release's files as it writes them, and checks the running release before it starts and the new one before and after the switch the way every start does, so an update takes about 30 seconds less on a full-size runtime. An install no longer reads every file it has just written again.

`delorun headless` without the API key its model needs (DeepSeek's unless the profile selects another provider) stops at once and says which variable to set or run `delorun setup key`, instead of linking the profile first and ending in a provider error. Its progress line goes to standard error, so standard output holds only the answer, and `delorun headless --help` no longer touches the profile.

A chat turn that starts before Delo's start check has finished no longer waits without a message: after 60 seconds the turn ends and says that the start check did not finish, that the message was not sent, and to start Delo with `delorun start` and send it again; `delorun status` and `delorun logs` show what the start is doing. This only happens when Delo was booted without `delorun`'s own start, or when the start's check never completes.

`delorun verify` lists the plugin changes you approved, by name and folder, then apart from them the changes that loaded without review, with protection off or while it was off, then everything present that you did not approve: changes waiting for your review and anything Changes does not find as it keeps it. Its summary line then never reads as a plain pass, and it exits 1 only when something is not as Changes keeps it. A run from a source checkout or a development build says there is no signed release to compare its files with.

`delorun doctor` reports your changes: the protection setting, any plugin you are working on, and for each plugin you link from a folder whether it loaded at the last start, whether it runs the content you approved or content that loaded without review, the dsh and Delo versions it requires and whether it changes a consent, a guard or the sandbox policy. When a plugin did not load or the start failed, it names the plugin and the change to undo.
A write lock left behind by a process that was killed while taking over a dead writer's lock no longer blocks later writers: the leftover claim is removed after ten seconds.
`delorun update` names why an automatic rollback did not finish. It blames the missing chat-data copy only when that is the reason, and otherwise says that going back stopped and where to look.

The release an update starts no longer inherits variables that load code into Node, its loader or OpenSSL, such as `NODE_OPTIONS` or `LD_PRELOAD`, even when a `.env` file set them for the running release; the launcher already dropped them from every start.

`delorun verify` hashes every runtime file before its own code runs, whatever the start check's record says, and then checks every file again. The record has no key, so a program running as you can rewrite it to hide a changed file, the runtime's Node and `delorun` itself included, from ordinary starts until the next full check, which comes at least every 7 days; `delorun verify` still finds it.
Delo's own changes are carried onto a newer DeepSeek Harness release by a maintainer command, which stops with a report of what no longer applies instead of dropping a change.

Delo records a checksum for each DeepSeek Harness file it edits, so the command notices when one of those files changed underneath it and refuses to carry a change that was edited after it was recorded.
`delorun --version` prints which Delo this is and which DeepSeek Harness it runs on, one line each, and `--json` prints the same two as one line for scripts.

A plugin can say which Delo versions it works with, and Delo honours it: a plugin that asks for a newer Delo than the one you run is refused at install and disabled at start, and the message tells you which Delo you have and which DeepSeek Harness it runs on. A plugin that asks for nothing behaves exactly as before.
Settings names Delo's version and, beneath it, the DeepSeek Harness version it runs on.

`delorun plugin check <folder>` tells a plugin author, without running the plugin, what its declared DeepSeek Harness and Delo versions allow on the Delo you run, what it leaves undeclared, and which Delo range to declare to target this release; Delo's documentation states what each Delo version promises a plugin.

A script that changes something through a Host's HTTP API over plain HTTP at an address other than this computer's, such as a name in `trustedHosts` or the address the Host listens on, must send an `Origin` header naming that address, such as `Origin: http://192.0.2.5:3080`; without one the Host answers "forbidden", because a web page could send the same request. Requests on this computer, over HTTPS and from the studio itself are unaffected.

The Host answers "bad request" to a request with more than one `Host` header, on every address it serves, and holds a request for a path such as `/x/../api/...` to the same rules as one for `/api/...`.

A script, or the desktop app's own requests, that talks to a Delo Host on the same computer with the Host's cookie is accepted again; the Host had answered "forbidden" to any request that changes something and states no origin. A request from a web page on another site or another local port is still refused.
